## The three models clarified

Let me separate them cleanly because I think you're blending them:

### Model 1: OSA Network (affiliated brokers under OSA's umbrella)
- Broker operates under OSA's Part 295, OSA's brand, OSA's tools
- No upfront fee, 50/50 commission split
- OSA holds the client relationship
- Example: eXp Realty agent model
- **Not SaaS. Clean moat.**

### Model 2: Dumont SaaS to independent brokerages
- Independent brokerage keeps their own Part 295 and brand
- They license Dumont as a software tool, pay monthly/per-seat
- They compete with OSA's direct brokerage in the market
- Example: Hamilton AI's current model
- **This is SaaS to competitors. Structural conflict.**

### Model 3: OSA Pay as industry payment infrastructure
- Independent brokerages keep their own Part 295 and brand
- They use OSA Pay for settlement, escrow, and compliance
- OSA takes 2% on every transaction settled through the rail
- Every transaction feeds OSA's data platform (volume, prices, operator performance)
- Example: Stripe Connect for small businesses, or Tuvoli (minus the structural conflict since OSA doesn't own aircraft)
- **Not SaaS. This is payment infrastructure. Different category entirely.**

## Here's the important clarification

**Model 1 and Model 3 are compatible with each other and with the full-stack thesis. Model 2 is not.**

You can absolutely do Model 1 (affiliated brokers under OSA) AND Model 3 (payment rail open to the industry) simultaneously. Those actually reinforce each other:

- Your own brokers use OSA Pay (gives you volume)
- Your affiliated brokers use OSA Pay (gives you more volume)
- Independent non-OSA brokerages use OSA Pay (gives you industry-wide volume)
- All of the above feed OSA's transaction data platform
- The data platform makes your *own* deals smarter
- Which makes your direct brokerage and affiliated broker deals win more often
- Which attracts more affiliated brokers
- Which gives the network more pull on operators
- Which makes OSA Pay more trusted
- Which makes more independents use it
- Flywheel.

**In Model 3, independent brokerages are not competitors — they're volume generators.** Because you're not selling them a tool that makes them better at competing against you. You're selling them settlement infrastructure that makes their deals faster and cheaper, and every deal on the rail gives you data you'd never get otherwise.

**Model 2 is the trap.** Dumont-as-SaaS-to-competitors. That's the one we said no to. And I still think you should say no to it.

Three consistent things emerged across all three VC lenses:

A brokerage network + payment infrastructure wrap is a $1-10B outcome because of the GMV × 2% × float math. That's what gets venture checks written.

**When you pitch, lead with the brokerage (to be credible). Close with payments (to be fundable).** Both are true. The order matters.

Not "why aviation" — you've got that. But specifically *why Phelipe is the one who wins*. VCs ask this for a reason: domain expertise is common, AI engineering is common, but the combination is rare. Your answer needs to be:

That's a compelling founder story if you articulate it. You haven't fully yet. You should.

## The part that matters most

VCs are pattern-matchers. They're looking for two things:
1. **Is the company shape recognizable as a big outcome?** Yes — your model matches Harvey, Lance, eXp, Airbnb, Stripe. Pattern-match is strong.
2. **Is the founder recognizable as someone who executes?** Unknown — you have zero deals. Pattern-match is weak.

The single thing you can do to convert "unknown" to "strong" is close deals. Not in the abstract. Specific deals with specific clients with specific revenue with specific operator feedback. One closed deal changes the entire VC conversation.

You said you can't close deal #1 yet because you don't have the contracts. That's true. But there are two workarounds that sophisticated founders use in your position:

**Workaround 1: Subcontract the first 5 deals through an existing Part 295 broker.** You find a friendly small broker, propose a white-label deal: you generate the leads, Dumont does the sourcing and quoting, they handle the contract and compliance, you split commission. You get to close deals *today* using their Part 295. The deals are real. The testimonials are real. The Dumont data is real. Once you have 5 like that, you get your own Part 295 and start transitioning to fully OSA-branded.

**Workaround 2: Close your first deal as an advisor / consultant.** You get paid for using Dumont to help a client find a trip, but the actual booking happens through an existing broker for the compliance reason. Not glamorous but it gets money in and proves the workflow.

Both are ways to start the deal flywheel even before your own Part 295 is active. Talk to a lawyer about whether the specifics work in your state, but the patterns are standard in other brokerage industries (real estate agents "hang their license" with established brokers, mortgage originators work under sponsoring lenders, etc.).

# TAM / SAM / SOM for OSA — Done Honestly

## Ground rules before I start

Three commitments for this exercise:

1. **Every number cited to a real source with a real year.** No "industry estimates say." If I don't have a source, I say I'm estimating and explain the math.

2. **TAM is not aspiration. TAM is the ceiling of what's theoretically capturable. SAM is what you can realistically address. SOM is what you will actually capture in the next 3-5 years.** Founders collapse these. VCs unpack them.

3. **I will point out when the numbers are wrong, inflated, or not comparable.** Your prior TAM work mixes revenue-volume with commission-pool. Those are different things. I'll separate them.

## The critical distinction that most TAM analyses screw up

Before I give you numbers, we have to be explicit about **which TAM we're measuring**:

- **Transaction TAM** = total dollar volume of all aviation transactions (charter + aircraft + payments). This is big and impressive but mostly *not yours* — the operators and sellers capture most of that.
- **Addressable fee pool TAM** = the sliver of that transaction volume that goes to brokers, advisors, and payment processors. *This is what you can capture.*

When legacy pitch decks say "private aviation is a $150B market," they mean transaction volume. Investors in 2026 know this trick and will discount you for using it. Sophisticated investors want the fee pool.

I'll give you both, clearly labeled, so you can use whichever is appropriate for your audience.

## Segment 1: Private Charter Brokerage (your Phase 1 wedge)

### Transaction TAM
- Global private jet charter services: **$27-29B (2025)**, projected $40-45B by 2030 at 8-13.5% CAGR
- US share: ~45% = **~$13B (2025)**

### Fee Pool TAM (what brokers actually earn)
- Brokered portion of charter: ~40-50% of all charter trips go through brokers vs. direct-to-operator. Industry sources vary; use 45% midpoint.
- US brokered charter volume: $13B × 45% = **~$5.85B (2025)**
- Broker commission rate: 10-16% (Paramount discloses 10-16%, industry average ~12%)
- **US Charter Broker Fee Pool: ~$700M-$940M/year (2025)**

That's your actual TAM for charter brokerage, honestly.

### SAM (Serviceable Addressable Market)
What you can realistically address given geography, client type, and service model:

- **Geography:** US-only for Year 1-3. Domestic + Canada + Caribbean eventually. International = Year 5+. Cuts to ~$700M.
- **Client segment:** Post-raise founders + corporate clients doing 2-8 trips/year (your locked beachhead). That's maybe 30-40% of the brokered charter market. Cuts to ~$210-280M.
- **Trip type:** Focus on KMDW hub + major corridors initially, then national. Light/mid/super-mid jets primarily. That's ~60% of brokered charter. Cuts to ~$125-170M.

**Charter SAM: ~$125-170M annual commission pool.**

### SOM (Serviceable Obtainable Market, 3-year window)
What OSA can actually capture by 2029 — and this is where honesty matters.

- Average deal size: $28K
- Average OSA commission: ~$3,500 per deal (12.5%)
- **Year 1 (you solo):** 20 deals closed at $3,500 = **$70K revenue**. 0.04% of SAM.
- **Year 2 (you + first affiliated brokers):** 5 brokers × 15 deals/year each + 30 of your own = 105 deals × $3,500 = **$367K revenue** (+ 50% commission share on affiliate deals, so actual OSA revenue ~$230K)
- **Year 3 (network active):** 15 brokers + you = ~400 deals × $3,500 = **$1.4M revenue**, OSA take ~$875K
- **Year 5 (scaled network):** 50 brokers doing 800 deals/year, $2.8M average broker commission pool, OSA takes ~$1.4M from commissions + deal #1 expansion

**Realistic Charter SOM by Year 3: $875K-$1.5M ARR.** By Year 5: $3-5M ARR.

That's the honest number. It's not glamorous. It's why charter brokerage alone isn't a venture business. It's a training ground.

## Claude

Good question to ask — it's actually quite relevant to what you're building, more than you might realize. Let me explain it cleanly.

## What Opendoor does

Opendoor is an **iBuyer** — they buy homes directly from sellers, renovate lightly, and resell them on the open market. "iBuyer" = instant buyer. The whole pitch to sellers is: *"Skip the 45-day MLS listing process, the showings, the negotiations. We'll give you a cash offer in 24 hours and close in a week."*

The seller trades off two things for that convenience:
1. A lower price than they'd probably get on the open market (Opendoor discounts 5-10% vs. peak retail)
2. A service fee to Opendoor (historically 5-14%, averaging around 7%)

Opendoor then holds the house for 30-90 days on average, does minor improvements ($5-15K), and relists it at market price plus their margin.

## How they actually make money

Four revenue streams, stacked:

**1. Spread (the core mechanic):** Buy at ~$400K, sell at ~$440K after costs. That $40K spread is the fundamental profit engine — about 8-10% of the home value when it works.

**2. Service fee charged to the seller:** 5-14% of home price, averaging ~7%. This is pure margin on the transaction itself, separate from the spread.

**3. Adjacent services:** Title insurance, escrow, home warranty, mortgage origination. They cross-sell financial products on both sides of the transaction.

**4. Data and pricing algorithm:** Their proprietary pricing model (the thing that decides "we'll pay exactly $412,000 for this house in Phoenix") is their core IP. Every transaction improves it.

## Why I'm bringing this up — the relevant part for OSA

Opendoor is instructive for you for three specific reasons, and one cautionary reason.

### Relevant parallel 1: They're a "full-stack marketplace" that owns the transaction

Opendoor doesn't license their pricing algorithm to other real estate agents. They don't sell "iBuying-as-a-Service" to Zillow or Redfin. They *are* the buyer. They capture the full transaction spread because they're the principal, not the agent.

Sound familiar? That's exactly the Model 1 discipline you locked earlier. Opendoor is the real estate version of what you're building — *be the transaction, not the tool.*

### Relevant parallel 2: Their moat is algorithmic pricing + data + speed

The core Opendoor edge is: given a house, how accurately can we price it in 24 hours? That's a data science problem. Their data platform (every house they've seen, every sale, every renovation cost) is the moat. The more transactions they do, the better the model gets.

Your OSA Data Platform + Ghost Positioning + Charter Index is the aviation version of this. Dumont's ability to price a charter in 90 seconds and source the right operator is structurally the same bet: **speed + proprietary data + algorithmic precision = unfair advantage.**

### Relevant parallel 3: They expanded into adjacent financial products

Once Opendoor had the transaction flow, they added title, escrow, mortgage, warranty. Each new product rides on top of transactions they were already capturing. OSA Pay is exactly this move — once you own the deal flow, payment infrastructure becomes obvious.

### The cautionary part — why Opendoor almost died

Here's the part you need to understand because it's genuinely a risk pattern OSA could fall into in one specific scenario.

**Opendoor nearly went bankrupt in 2022-2023.** Their stock dropped from $36 to under $1. Why?

Because their business model has a hidden structural problem: **they hold inventory.** When they buy a house, they own it until it sells. If the housing market turns — rates go up, prices drop, demand dries up — they get stuck holding hundreds of millions in depreciating inventory while still paying carrying costs (property tax, insurance, maintenance, interest on capital used to buy the homes).

Opendoor's problem is that their "spread" only works when home prices are going up or stable. When prices drop, they sell at a loss on every house. Q3 2022 they lost $928M in a single quarter because their algorithm priced homes based on a market that turned before they could sell.

**The lesson:** full-stack marketplaces that take principal risk (hold inventory, own transactions) get crushed when the market cycle turns against them. Agents and brokers (like Compass, Redfin, traditional realtors) don't have this problem — they get paid commission whether prices go up or down.

## Why this is relevant to OSA specifically

**You are deliberately not Opendoor, and that's your advantage.**

OSA never owns aircraft. You're a broker. You get commission when deals close, regardless of market direction. If private aviation demand drops 30% next year, your revenue drops proportionally — but you don't have $500M of aircraft inventory depreciating on a balance sheet.

This is why your earlier decision — *"permanently owning zero aircraft to maintain independence"* — is more strategically important than even you may have realized. That decision is what makes OSA uncorrelated with aviation market cycles in a way Opendoor is completely correlated with housing cycles.

## The one place to be careful

There's one version of OSA that becomes Opendoor-risky: **if OSA Pay ever extends credit to clients or advances payments to operators before client funds clear.**

The moment you go from "we hold funds in escrow" to "we front the operator and collect from the client later," you're taking principal risk on the balance sheet. That's where aviation fintechs get in trouble. Tuvoli explicitly doesn't do this. Stripe's charter-adjacent processors don't do this. It's a line you shouldn't cross without very deliberate capitalization and risk modeling.

When VCs eventually push you toward "but if you just extended credit, your take rate could be 5% instead of 2%..." — that's the Opendoor pitch. Don't take it without real fintech infrastructure and a real balance sheet.

## Quick side-by-side

| Dimension | Opendoor | OSA |
|---|---|---|
| Business type | iBuyer (principal) | Broker (agent) |
| Holds inventory | Yes (houses) | No (never aircraft) |
| Revenue model | Spread + service fee + financial products | Commission + payment processing + float |
| Market cycle risk | Very high (got crushed 2022) | Low (commission-based) |
| Data moat | Pricing algorithm across transactions | Pricing algorithm across deals + operator data |
| Expansion path | Title → mortgage → insurance | OSA Pay → escrow → aircraft advisory |
| Bad outcome | Bankruptcy if market turns | Slower growth in a downturn, not existential |

## The takeaway

Opendoor is instructive because it shows you what happens when you combine AI-native pricing with transaction capture in a fragmented legacy market — *it can be a $15B company at peak*. But it also shows you the risk of taking principal positions on the underlying asset.

OSA gets to capture the intelligence layer and the transaction flow **without** the balance sheet exposure. That's a structurally better business than Opendoor's. Same moat pattern, lower risk profile.

When a VC asks "who are you like?" — Opendoor is a useful answer with the caveat *"but without the inventory risk."* That's a sophisticated framing.

What made you ask about Opendoor? Is there a specific mechanic from their model you're wondering about?

## I misled you on the Part 295 timeline

I said "6+ month process." That's not accurate. Here's what's actually true:

### Part 295 is a registration, not a license

Critical distinction. "License" implies approval, examinations, vetting, a waiting period. Part 295 is **registration** — you file paperwork with DOT's Office of Aviation Analysis and you're registered. There's no approval queue, no test, no waiting period for DOT to decide you're qualified.

No federal license is required in the US. Brokers who hold client funds must register under DOT Part 295 regulations. No FAA certificate is needed — that is required only of the operators who fly the aircraft.

Part 295 does not require a broker to take any courses, or become licensed or certified

The entire aviation industry jokes about this. the industry joke has been that you can be a broker by buying a cell phone, a laptop and a desk, set up a simple five-page website for a few hundred dollars, and work from your closet... there is no licensing and regulations, so just about anyone can do it under the radar including convicted felons

The barrier to *becoming* a charter broker is almost nothing. The barrier to becoming a *good* one is everything. Part 295 was specifically created in 2019 to add minimum transparency rules, not to gate entry.

### What you actually have to do

Per the actual regulation and the DOT Office of Aviation Analysis process:

1. **Register with DOT Office of Aviation Analysis** — submit legal/trade names, business address, owners, key personnel. Paperwork, not approval.
2. **Get liability insurance** — your choice of coverage level; you must disclose whether you have it and at what limits.
3. **Draft compliant disclosure templates** — what you must tell clients before contracting (broker status, total cost breakdown, refund policy, etc.).
4. **Maintain recordkeeping** — ongoing, for audit.

That's it. No exam. No approval. No certificate.

### The realistic timeline

Total time from decision to operating legally: **2-6 weeks**, not 6 months. Breakdown:

- Register LLC / entity (you already have OSA as Delaware C-Corp): done
- DOT registration paperwork filing: 1-2 weeks to prepare, days to file
- Insurance: 1-3 weeks to shop, bind, and issue certificates
- Disclosure templates and contracts: 1-2 weeks with a lawyer
- Bank account and basic operations: parallel, days to weeks

If you pushed, you could be operating legally in 3 weeks. Taking your time: 6-8 weeks comfortably. Not 6 months.

### Cost

Start costs: $5K-15K

That range is for a fully legitimate solo brokerage setup. Your incremental cost on top of what OSA already has (LLC, some infrastructure): probably $3-8K for DOT filing help, insurance premiums for year one, and contract templates.

### Where I was half-right

The insurance piece has some real work. You need:
- General liability
- E&O (errors and omissions) — the important one for brokers
- Possibly cyber / tech E&O given AI use

Insurance takes 2-4 weeks to shop properly. Underwriters will want to see your disclosure templates, your business plan, and your risk management. Not because they're gating you, but because pricing depends on it. This is the piece that eats the most time and it's real.

### What this changes in the plan

Your Phase 1 → Phase 2 bottleneck isn't Part 295. **Part 295 is a 4-6 week task. The actual bottlenecks are:**

1. **Finding your first real client** — this is harder than the paperwork
2. **Having a Part 135 operator willing to quote you** — operators prefer working with brokers who have track records; being brand-new means some operators will ignore your RFQs until you prove volume
3. **Getting appropriate E&O insurance at reasonable cost** — brand-new broker with no history may pay more for coverage

The Part 295 filing itself is the easy part. The bottleneck is *market entry* — operators not taking you seriously, clients not knowing you exist, insurance underwriters being cautious. Those are real friction points but they're different from what I said.

### What I should have said in the scale system

Corrected Phase 1 → Phase 2 bottleneck: **"Operator network trust and first client acquisition, not paperwork. Part 295 registration is a 4-6 week task; the hard part is getting Part 135 operators to take a brand-new broker's RFQs seriously without an existing track record."**

That's the honest version.

### The practical next step for you

You probably don't need a 6-month runway to be operating. You need:
- 4-6 weeks of focused paperwork + insurance
- A good aviation attorney for disclosure templates (Garofalo Goerlich Hainbach PC is cited as the industry go-to; Dunaway Law Group also specializes in this)
- An E&O underwriter who knows aviation (Global Aerospace, USAIG, or Starr Aviation typically)

I'd estimate **$5-10K in setup costs and 6 weeks to legal operation**. Not 6 months.

I should have verified before throwing out "6+ months." That's the kind of number that shapes your whole roadmap and I should have either flagged uncertainty or searched first. ## The actual § 295.24 disclosures, straight from the regulation

Part 295 splits disclosures into two buckets. I flattened them earlier. Here's the accurate version:

### Three MANDATORY disclosures (must be provided before contract, no request needed)

Per § 295.24(a), paragraphs (1), (2), and (6):

1. **Operator identity (a)(1)** — The corporate name of the direct air carrier (or foreign direct air carrier) in operational control of the aircraft, plus any other names that carrier uses publicly.

2. **Broker capacity (a)(2)** — In what capacity the broker is acting when contracting for the air transportation:
 - As an indirect air carrier
 - As an indirect foreign air carrier
 - As an agent of the charterer
 - As an agent of the direct air carrier

3. **Liability insurance (a)(6)** — The existence or absence of liability insurance held by the broker covering the charterer, passengers, and property on the charter flight, and the monetary limits of any such insurance.

### Three DISCLOSURES UPON REQUEST (only if the charterer asks)

Per § 295.24(a), paragraphs (3), (4), and (5):

4. **Broker-carrier relationship (a)(3)** — If the broker is acting as the charterer's agent, any corporate or business relationship (including preexisting contracts) between the broker and the direct air carrier that may bear on carrier selection.

5. **Total cost (a)(4)** — The total cost of the air transportation paid by the charterer to or through the broker, including any broker or carrier-imposed fees or government-imposed taxes and fees. Itemization is optional.

6. **Third-party fees (a)(5)** — The existence and amounts of third-party fees (fuel, landing, parking, hangar) the charterer will pay directly.

## Where my earlier summary was wrong

I said "broker status, total cost breakdown, refund policy" as the mandatory disclosures. Let me correct each one:

- **"Broker status"** → Partially right. The capacity disclosure (a)(2) is mandatory, and the broker-vs-carrier-identification requirement also shows up in § 295.23 (advertising). But "broker status" is imprecise. The mandatory disclosure is the specific capacity (indirect air carrier vs agent of charterer vs agent of carrier). That distinction matters legally.

- **"Total cost breakdown"** → Wrong about it being mandatory. Total cost (a)(4) is only required **upon request** by the charterer. It's not an automatic disclosure.

- **"Refund policy"** → Wrong. Refund policy is not one of the § 295.24 disclosures at all. Refunds are handled separately under § 295.26 and cross-reference 14 CFR 374.3 and 12 CFR Part 226 for credit cards, and require refunds within 20 days for cash/check. But this is a compliance requirement, not a pre-contract disclosure.

What I missed entirely:
- **Liability insurance disclosure** — this is mandatory and I didn't mention it. You have to affirmatively state whether you have insurance and how much, before contracting.
- **Operator identity** — mandatory. You have to tell the client who the actual Part 135 carrier is before signing.

So the accurate mandatory list is: **operator identity, your capacity, and your insurance status.** The "upon request" list is: broker-carrier relationship, total cost, and third-party fees.

## Why the distinction matters for you specifically

This is not a trivial correction. Three practical consequences:

**1. Total cost disclosure being "upon request" gives you commercial flexibility.**
You're not *required* to break down cost before contract unless the client asks. That means you can quote a total price without disclosing your commission unless they ask. Paramount volunteers the 10-16% breakdown as a marketing differentiator — it's their choice. You can choose either approach. But you should decide this deliberately as a positioning choice, not because you think you're legally required.

**2. Operator identity is mandatory — this changes Dumont's workflow.**
Before any contract is signed, the specific operating carrier has to be disclosed. This means Dumont cannot generate a quote that contracts the client to a "trip" without naming the carrier. Every quote must identify the operator by corporate name. That's a workflow requirement — Dumont's output template must include this field and cannot skip it.

**3. Insurance disclosure is mandatory — this affects your Year 1 setup.**
You have to have a clear answer to "do you have liability insurance, and at what limits?" before you contract anything. This means insurance procurement isn't optional Year 1 paperwork you can defer — it's required before deal #1. Even if you say "no, we don't carry it" that disclosure itself is mandatory. Most brokers do carry it because saying "no" kills most deals.

## The problem, stated cleanly

Aviation operators don't stay still. Companies rebrand, get acquired, split, rename, fly under new Part 135 certificates. **Each event creates an identity discontinuity** — the same physical operation showing up in different datasets under different names at different times.

Concrete examples from your own data:

- **Aviation Advisor Inc. → Altivion Aviation** (rebrand, late 2025) — same legal entity, same Part 135 cert, same people, new name
- **Aero Ways Inc. → flyADVANCED** (rebrand, 2015)
- **Million Air Dallas → MAnext** (charter rebrand, 2025)
- **Jet Aviation** — many related entities under General Dynamics parent, all calling themselves "Jet Aviation something"
- **TAG Aviation Holding** — split in 1998 into TAG UK, TAG USA, TAG Cayman, TAG SM

Now the poison. Each dataset captures a **different snapshot at a different point in time:**

- **FAA registry** sees the current legal name on the Part 135 certificate
- **ARGUS** scrape from last Tuesday sees what ARGUS's directory showed last Tuesday
- **Wyvern** audit from 6 months ago sees the name as it was 6 months ago
- **ADS-B hex codes** are tied to the aircraft, not the operator — same plane flies under different operators over its lifetime
- **NTSB** attributes accidents to whatever the operator's name was at the time of the incident. **If the company rebrands after a crash, the crash stays on the OLD name.**

That last one is the killer. A broker or a client searches "Altivion Aviation" for safety history and gets a clean record. The 2020 NTSB fatal is still attributed to the pre-rebrand name. **Rebrands can launder safety records.** Classic Aviation (the investigation you did earlier) is an example of this pattern in the wild.

That's why your head is fuzzy. It's not one problem — it's the intersection of four problems:

1. **Identity resolution across datasets** (is "Altivion" the same as "Aviation Advisor" in the ARGUS scrape?)
2. **Temporal identity tracking** (when did the rebrand happen, and how do we show the continuity?)
3. **Claim preservation** (we cannot lose the fact that ARGUS originally said "Aviation Advisor" — that's historical truth we're not allowed to overwrite)
4. **Safety-record continuity** (the NTSB crash must transfer to the new canonical name even though NTSB still calls it by the old name)

## The solution, in two layers

### Layer 1: The data model (what you're building)

Three tables. This is the core pattern:

**`operators`** — the canonical entity, one row per real operator regardless of how many names it's had. Think of this as the "soul" of the company. Grand Teton Aviation / Altivion / Aviation Advisor all collapse into **one row** here.

**`operator_identities`** — every name-at-a-time observation from every source. One row per claim like:
- "ARGUS called this entity 'Aviation Advisor Inc.' on 2025-03-15"
- "Wyvern called this entity 'Altivion Aviation' on 2025-11-02"
- "FAA Part 135 cert shows 'Aviation Advisor Inc.' as legal name on 2025-09-01"

Each row carries provenance: source, date, match method, confidence score. **You never delete these.** They're the evidence trail.

**`operator_aliases`** — the explicit mapping of alternative names to the canonical operator. "Aviation Advisor" is an alias of the canonical Altivion row. Includes date ranges when possible ("called this from 2012-2025").

The rebrand itself gets captured as a separate event in **`operator_events`** (Stage 3 work) with a link: `REBRANDED_FROM Aviation Advisor Inc. → Altivion Aviation, effective 2025-11-XX, source: company announcement + trade press + FAA filing`.

The NTSB crash stays attached to whatever operator_identity existed at the time of the crash, but because that identity points at the canonical operator, **queries against the canonical operator surface the crash regardless of what it's currently called.** That's how you fix safety-record laundering.

### Layer 2: How decisions get made (the "researcher" idea)

Here's the part that's making you fuzzy, because it's subtle.

**You cannot let the matcher auto-merge based on string similarity alone.** "Global Aviation Inc." vs "Global Jet Capital" look similar — the matcher scored them 0.651. But one is a charter operator in Portland and the other is an aircraft financier in Connecticut. **Different companies, different functions.** Auto-merge would corrupt the canonical.

So you built a three-tier system:

**Auto-merge tier (high confidence, ≥0.85 match score + multiple signals agreeing):** Matcher commits the merge automatically. These are safe bets like "ABC Aviation LLC" matching "ABC Aviation" when address and certificate number also match.

**Review tier (mid confidence, 0.60-0.85):** Goes into `operator_match_review`. A human (you, for now) decides. This is where the actual judgment lives. Aviation Advisor → Altivion scored low because the strings look completely different, but it's a correct match. Only domain knowledge reveals that.

**Reject tier (low confidence, <0.60):** Does not get proposed. These are dropped or flagged as new operators needing investigation.

**Now the researcher idea.** You cannot personally review every pair. You need a "researcher" — an agent that does what you were doing manually in the Classic Aviation investigation: web search, company filings, trade press, ARGUS listings, cross-reference beneficial ownership, resolve the identity.

The implementation pattern for the researcher, based on what you've been building:

1. **Review queue item arrives** ("Is Aviation Advisor Inc. = Altivion Aviation?")
2. **Researcher agent runs Firecrawl/web_search** on both entity names
3. **Researcher synthesizes evidence**: press releases, state filings, Part 135 certificate numbers, company addresses, personnel overlap
4. **Multi-model verification for Gold merges**: the proposal goes through Opus + Sonnet + GPT. If they agree, higher confidence. If they disagree, human review.
5. **Researcher writes a proposal** with evidence bundle: "Proposed: MERGE. Evidence: (a) trade press announcement dated X, (b) FAA registry shows same ICAO code, (c) beneficial owner overlap, (d) address continuity. Confidence: 0.92."
6. **Proposal either auto-applies (if confidence ≥ threshold + Two-Source Rule satisfied) or goes to you for final review.**

The **Two-Source Rule** is critical: for Gold-tier events like rebrand merges, you need at least two independent sources confirming. One press release is not enough. One FAA filing is not enough. Two or more, from different source types (press + regulatory, or press + company + audit), before it lands in Gold.

## Why this works

The whole design has one philosophical commitment: **the graph never deletes claims.**

When ARGUS originally scraped "Aviation Advisor Inc." that was true at that moment. You do not erase it. You attach it to the canonical Altivion operator as a historical identity, with dates, and the system knows both are the same underlying entity while preserving the evidence that the name changed.

This is what makes OSA's data moat different from JETNET's. JETNET's researchers manually called operators and wrote notes. You're building an agent that does the same research with structured provenance, multi-model verification, and permanent audit trails. Every decision is reconstructable years later.

The fuzziness in your head is because you're carrying all four problems (identity + time + claims + safety) in memory at once and trying to reason about them as one thing. The solution is that the data model separates them into distinct tables with distinct lifecycles, and the researcher agent automates the judgment that currently requires you.

## What's actually blocking you right now

Two things, based on what I'm seeing in the conversation trail:

1. **The review queue has 74 pending items and growing.** You cannot personally review them all. The researcher agent is the unblocker, but it's not fully built yet.

2. **Stage 3 (operator_events, temporal edges) isn't built yet.** The current schema handles identities but not the rebrand events themselves as first-class graph objects. Altivion and Aviation Advisor can be linked by alias, but the *event* (REBRANDED_TO, 2025-11-XX, with its own evidence bundle) isn't represented yet. That's the next architectural piece.

Both are solvable. Neither is philosophical. Your architecture is sound — the constitution in the ER plan holds up. You're just mid-build on a hard problem.

## The simpler mental model you can hold

When you feel fuzzy again, come back to this:

- **One operator, many names, over time.** That's the whole problem.
- **The canonical is the soul. The identities are the masks.** Never delete masks; always point them at the right soul.
- **Events are how souls change names.** Rebrands, acquisitions, splits — each is a first-class event with evidence.
- **The researcher does what you were doing by hand. Provenance is how you trust the researcher.**
- **Two independent sources minimum before anything lands in Gold.**

## Palantir Foundry's Ontology — the structure

Palantir's Ontology is the commercial version of exactly the pattern you're building. In their own words:

An Ontology is a categorization of the world. In Foundry, the Ontology is the digital twin of an organization, a rich semantic layer that sits on top of the digital assets (datasets and models) integrated into Foundry. The Foundry Ontology creates a complete picture of an organization's world by mapping datasets and models to object types, properties, link types, and action types.

The four concepts:

- **Object type** = the kind of real-world thing (Employee, Aircraft, Order, Operator)
- **Property** = what that thing has (name, date, certificate number)
- **Link type** = how it connects to other things (employs, owns, operates, rebrands_to)
- **Action type** = how it can change (hire, rebrand, acquire, deactivate)

Translate that directly to OSA's ER:

- **Object type** = Operator, Aircraft, Identity, Event, Route, Client
- **Property** = legal name, Part 135 cert number, address, ARGUS rating
- **Link type** = rebranded_to, acquired_by, operates_aircraft, subsidiary_of
- **Action type** = merge_identities, record_rebrand_event, update_trust_score

This is exactly your operators / operator_identities / operator_aliases / operator_events / relationships model. You landed on the right pattern through first principles. Palantir sells it as software for $1M-$10M per deployment. **You built the aviation-specific version.**

## Where your system and Palantir's diverge

Here's the part that matters for you strategically.

### What Palantir does

Palantir Foundry is **generic ontology infrastructure.** It's a platform. Customers (governments, banks, oil companies, manufacturers, hospitals) bring their own data and model their own domain. Palantir provides the tools to define object types, link datasets, run ER, enforce security. **They don't know anything about aviation.** Their customers teach the ontology what their world looks like.

Palantir's commercial value is the platform itself. Implementation consultants — called Forward Deployed Engineers — spend months with each customer mapping datasets to objects, tuning ER, building workflows. The ontology becomes the digital twin of that specific organization.

Surf Air is using Palantir Foundry (we covered this earlier — the $26M SurfOS spend). That's what BrokerOS is under the hood: Palantir ontology + aviation data + Surf's custom workflows.

### What you're doing differently

You're building a **pre-modeled, aviation-specific ontology** with domain intelligence baked in.

Palantir can't tell you that "Aviation Advisor Inc. → Altivion Aviation" is a rebrand. It can give you the tools to model it once you've figured it out. **You're building a system that figures it out.** Your researcher agent is doing the epistemic work Palantir leaves to humans.

The delta is:

| Dimension | Palantir Foundry | OSA ER Platform |
|---|---|---|
| Ontology | Generic, customer-modeled | Aviation-specific, pre-modeled |
| ER decisions | Human Forward Deployed Engineers | AI researcher agent + HITL for Gold |
| Domain knowledge | Lives in the customer's head | Lives in the Claude.md, writing-guide, aircraft-scoring, researcher prompt |
| Sale model | Platform license + FDE services | (not for sale — you are the customer) |
| Data freshness | Customer updates on their cadence | Continuous ADS-B + scraping + agent refresh |
| Cost to deploy | $1M-$10M+ | Your build time |

The key insight: **Palantir is horizontal infrastructure. OSA is a vertical digital twin.** Palantir enables digital twins. You are one.

This is also why OSA's moat is real against Surf-on-Palantir. Surf has Palantir's excellent platform plus airline operational data. They don't have the pre-modeled aviation ontology with cross-dataset ER and rebrand tracking that you're building. Their ontology is their operational data. Yours is the industry.

## The researcher pattern — how it fits

You nailed this intuition. The researcher in your ER system is the aviation-specific version of what Palantir calls a Forward Deployed Engineer combined with what they call an Ontology Action.

In Palantir's world, when a potential merge surfaces in the ER pipeline, a human FDE investigates, gathers evidence, and proposes an Action (merge, link, update). The Action writes to the ontology with provenance.

In your system, the researcher agent:

1. Receives a candidate pair from `operator_match_review`
2. Runs web_search + Firecrawl on both entity names
3. Pulls FAA registry lookups, state filings, trade press
4. Synthesizes evidence with multi-model verification (Opus + Sonnet + GPT consensus)
5. Writes a proposal: MERGE / SPLIT / NEW_OPERATOR / REJECT with evidence bundle and confidence score
6. Auto-applies if confidence is high + Two-Source Rule satisfied
7. Escalates to you if below threshold

**It's FDE-as-code.** You encode the research workflow once, and it runs against every pair that lands in review. The domain knowledge that would live in an FDE's head lives in the prompt, the tool configuration, and the evidence rubric.

This is also why your approach scales economically in a way Palantir's doesn't. Palantir needs an FDE per customer per deployment. You need one well-designed researcher agent that handles every ER decision across the entire aviation industry forever.

## The way to explain this to a VC

When someone asks "how is your data moat different from what Palantir offers to Surf?" the answer is:

*"Palantir is horizontal ontology infrastructure. It requires a human Forward Deployed Engineer to model each customer's domain and resolve ambiguous entities. We built a vertical, aviation-specific digital twin with an AI researcher agent that does the entity resolution work FDEs do at Palantir — but continuously, at scale, with multi-model verification and full provenance. Surf has Palantir's platform; we are the aviation industry's digital twin."*

That framing does two things simultaneously:

1. Positions you as *more sophisticated* than a Palantir implementation in the aviation domain, not competing with Palantir generally
2. Makes clear why your ER moat compounds — every review queue decision trains the researcher, every merge event becomes precedent for the next one, every dataset addition gets resolved against a graph that already knows the industry

## The papers that matter for what you're doing

I'm going to stop talking around this and give you the five actual academic papers that are directly relevant. These aren't vendor docs. These are peer-reviewed or arXiv research, and your ER architecture is consistent with them.

### 1. The paper closest to your researcher pattern

**"Multi-Agent RAG Framework for Entity Resolution: Advancing Beyond Single-LLM Approaches with Specialized Agent Coordination"** (MDPI Computers, December 2025)

This is the one. Published three months ago. It describes almost exactly the system you're building.

Their setup: four specialized agents — Direct Agent for name-based matching, Indirect Agent for transitive linkage, Household Agent for clustering, Move Detector for tracking relocations across time. Built on LangGraph. Each agent uses retrieval-augmented generation to ground its reasoning in verifiable evidence.

Their findings: 94.3% accuracy on name variations, complete decision transparency, and a 61% reduction in API calls compared to single-LLM approaches.

Why this maps to you: swap "household" for "operator" and "residential movement" for "rebrand/acquisition," and it's your architecture. Specialized agents instead of one monolithic LLM. Retrieval grounding for evidence. Complete provenance. That's exactly what you and I designed for the reviewer queue.

Full citation and repo: *Computers 14(12), 525, 2025.* [mdpi.com/2073-431X/14/12/525](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/14/12/525). Code at [github.com/Aatif123-hub/Household-Discovery-using-Multi-Agents](https://github.com/Aatif123-hub/Household-Discovery-using-Multi-Agents)

### 2. The cost-efficiency paper that justifies your HITL pattern

**"On Leveraging Large Language Models for Enhancing Entity Resolution: A Cost-efficient Approach"** (Li et al., arXiv 2401.03426, January 2024)

The problem they solve is exactly your problem: LLM API calls are expensive, so you can't run every possible match through them. Their solution: an uncertainty reduction framework using LLMs to improve entity resolution results. We first initialize possible partitions of the entity cluster... Then, we reduce the uncertainty by selecting a few valuable matching questions for LLM verification. Upon receiving the answers, we update the probability distribution of the possible partitions.

Translation: you don't run the LLM on every pair. You run it only on the pairs where the LLM's answer will most reduce total uncertainty. That's your three-tier threshold (auto-merge / review / reject) — it's formally the same optimization.

They also mention it's called **BoostER** in some secondary sources. Same paper, same framework.

Link: [arxiv.org/abs/2401.03426](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.03426)

### 3. The knowledge graph paper covering your multi-model debate pattern

**KARMA and AutoKG frameworks** — referenced in "Statistical Network Analysis for LLMs via Knowledge Graphs" (2025)

Zhu et al. (2024) extended this approach to multi-agent ensembles in their AutoKG framework, where different LLMs (e.g., GPT-4, ChatGPT) are prompted separately, and their outputs are reconciled into consistent triples. Similarly, Lu and Wang (2025) advanced this paradigm with the KARMA framework, leveraging multi-agent LLMs for automated KG enrichment through entity discovery, relation extraction, and conflict resolution via multi-layer verification to reduce discrepancies.

This is the academic basis for the "Opus + Sonnet + GPT consensus for Gold merges" rule in your ER plan. KARMA specifically uses multi-layer verification across different LLMs to reduce discrepancies. That's your pattern, with a name.

### 4. The provenance paper that backs your Two-Source Rule

**"LLM Agents for Interactive Workflow Provenance: Reference Architecture and Evaluation Methodology"** (arXiv 2509.13978, September 2025)

This one's from LBNL and covers the architectural patterns for making LLM agents that capture provenance — why a decision was made, what evidence was used, how to replay it later. Critical for your "the graph never deletes claims" principle and your requirement that every ER decision carries its evidence bundle.

RAG Strategies. A common RAG use case is accessing data from an external database; here, the raw provenance data. Strategies include: No data (no provenance in the prompt), Partial data (a relevant subset), and Full data (entire database).

The methodology section of this paper is worth reading before you finalize the researcher agent prompt. It tells you how to evaluate whether your researcher's outputs are actually traceable and reproducible — not just plausible-sounding.

Link: [arxiv.org/abs/2509.13978](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.13978)

### 5. The foundational paper on semantic entity resolution

**"Grale: Designing Networks for Graph Learning"** (Halcrow et al., NeurIPS 2020)

This is the Google paper that proved semantic methods for entity resolution can scale. It's pre-LLM (uses graph embeddings) but it's the foundational work that everything since has built on. Towards Data Science summarizes it: Matching in entity resolution for knowledge graphs is just link prediction of SAME_AS edges, a common graph machine learning task. There is little question that semantic clustering for link prediction can cost-efficiently scale, as the technique was proven at Google by Google Grale.

If you wanted one "foundational" citation for a VC pitch explaining the academic basis, this is it. Google-scale proof that semantic ER works.

## The actual story — Jeff Jonas and 40 years of ER

Jonas is the closest thing entity resolution has to a founding figure. The arc:

- **1980s** — founded Systems Research & Development (SRD) in Las Vegas. Built "Non-Obvious Relationship Awareness" (NORA) for casinos. His work also helped identify the MIT card-counting team as brought to life in the book "Bringing Down the House" and film "21."
- **2001** — In-Q-Tel (CIA venture arm) invests in NORA
- **2005** — IBM acquires SRD
- **2008-2009** — Jonas starts the G2 skunkworks at IBM. The 'G' in G2 stands for Genus – because compared to every other branch of ER, it's a different species entirely.
- **2012** — IBM ships G2 commercially as InfoSphere Sensemaking
- **2016** — IBM spins G2 out as Senzing
- **2018** — Senzing launches publicly
- **2025-2026** — Senzing ships **Agentic Entity Resolution** with MCP server

That last bullet is the one you need to focus on. Senzing just shipped the AI-agent-era version of what they've been doing for 40 years. As autonomous AI agents reshape the world, Jonas is re-defining ER yet again. Without an understanding of who is who and who is related to whom, AI cannot deliver trusted, actionable insights. Senzing is the first to bring Agentic Entity Resolution to market – requiring 100x-1,000x less human effort to combine new data sources and operate entity resolution at scale. With the Senzing MCP Server, both humans and AI agents can deploy, feed, analyze, and publish identity insights entirely conversationally.

**That's shipping product, not theory.** Senzing MCP Server. Your Dumont MCP could talk to Senzing's MCP for ER queries today, potentially.

Now let me explain why their approach is philosophically different from what you're building, and then how to combine both — because that's where the real answer is.

## Senzing's core philosophy — "principle-based ER"

This is the breakthrough. Jonas's system doesn't use:
- Rules (that humans write and maintain)
- Training data (that humans label)
- Large language models (that hallucinate)

Instead Senzing uses **principle-based algorithms with built-in cultural knowledge.** Senzing AI cannot hallucinate. It is not generative and doesn't rely on large language models. Instead, Senzing AI delivers consistent, explainable, real-time entity resolution with unprecedented accuracy and scale.

What they built in is wild: 850 million global names and culturally aware name-matching logic, advanced comparators for global addresses, phone numbers, dates, Social Security numbers, and more.

And the operational principles that make it work are:

**1. Full Attribution (your Two-Source Rule, industrialized)**
There are no processes (e.g., merge/purge, data survivorship) whereby some data is discarded. That is because if data is discarded, system-to-system reconciliation audits become problematic. Moreover, if a system incorrectly discards information, it becomes difficult or impossible to correct such historical decisions.

This is exactly your principle: *the graph never deletes claims.* Jonas figured this out in the 1990s from casino fraud work. You arrived at it from first principles. Same conclusion.

**2. Sequence Neutrality**

Senzing can process records in any order and reach the same answer. If a later record contradicts an earlier merge, the system self-corrects — it doesn't matter which came first. This is **critical** for you. Your review queue processes pairs as they arrive. Senzing's approach says: don't lock in a decision just because it's chronologically first. If ADS-B data in 2027 reveals that Altivion and some other operator are actually the same fleet, the system should be able to restructure the entity graph retroactively.

**3. Self-correction on new evidence**

Every new record can update prior decisions. Self-corrects and learns in real time on your own data sets as new data arrives. That's continuous ER, not batch ER.

**4. Data Tethering**

Adds, changes and deletes occurring in systems of record must be accounted for in as close to real time as possible. Data currentness is significant, especially if one is making important, difficult to reverse, decisions that affect people's freedoms or privileges.

For you: when an operator's certificate gets suspended, that has to propagate through the graph immediately. Not daily. Real-time.

**5. Field Hashing (privacy-preserving ER)**

They can do ER on cryptographically hashed data. Operators could participate in your graph without giving up raw customer lists — their hashed customer data could still be matched for duplicate detection. This matters later for the affiliated broker network.

## Why this changes my earlier advice

I told you to build the researcher agent with LLMs (Opus + Sonnet + GPT consensus). That's still correct for the *judgment-heavy, evidence-gathering* part — rebrands, mergers, corporate intent, press release synthesis.

But for the **mechanical ER of names, addresses, phone numbers, Part 135 cert numbers** — the pattern-matching across 295 operator_identities rows looking for duplicates — **LLMs are wrong tool.** They're slow, expensive, non-deterministic, and can't explain decisions consistently.

What Jonas figured out 20 years ago: **you don't need an LLM for "ABC Aviation LLC" matching "ABC Aviation Inc."** You need a principled comparator that understands company-suffix equivalence, name transliteration, address normalization, phone format variation. That's math and domain knowledge, not reasoning.

**The correct architecture for you is a hybrid:**

- **Mechanical ER layer** = Senzing-style principle-based comparators. Handles 80-90% of matches deterministically, instantly, with full provenance. No LLM calls.
- **Semantic ER layer** = Multi-agent LLM researcher. Handles the 10-20% that need judgment — rebrands, mergers, corporate identity chains, industry knowledge.
- **Graph layer** = Stores the resolved entities, relationships, events, provenance. Queryable by Dumont and humans.

### Option B: Build Senzing-style principles yourself

Implement principle-based comparators in your codebase. Name normalization, cert number comparison, address canonicalization, corporate suffix handling, transliteration.

**Pros:**
- Full control.
- No vendor lock-in.
- Aviation-specific from day one.

**Cons:**

- Time you spend on this is time not spent closing deals.

### Option C: Hybrid — my actual recommendation

**Use Senzing for the mechanical layer. Build your aviation-specific researcher agent on top.**

Specifically:

1. **Senzing handles**: operator name dedup, address matching, phone normalization, basic fuzzy matching across operator_identities. Returns candidate matches with confidence scores.

2. **Your code handles**: aviation-specific features Senzing doesn't know — Part 135 cert number comparison, ICAO code cross-reference, ADS-B hex code correlation, safety rating alignment across ARGUS/Wyvern.

3. **Your researcher agent handles**: the judgment calls Senzing can't make — "is this a rebrand or a coincidence?" Multi-source web research, LLM synthesis, multi-model consensus for Gold merges.

4. **Your graph layer stores**: the resolved entities, events, provenance, relationships.

This is actually how Jonas describes the future. Senzing's MCP server exists exactly so AI agents can call ER as a service. You're not competing with Senzing — you're standing on their shoulders and building the aviation-domain intelligence layer that doesn't exist anywhere else.

## Claude

Great question, and I want to answer it honestly because there's a real answer and then there's a hype answer. I'm going to give you the real one.

## The short answer

**Yes, you can build an ER for each of the 1,821 operators working backwards in time. No, you cannot get to 100% identity resolution. You can realistically get to 92-97% with the right datasets, and the last 3-8% will always require judgment calls where multiple equally-defensible answers exist.**

Let me break down why, what datasets actually get you there, and where the ceiling is.

## The "go backwards from the current list" approach — this is actually the right method

It's called **temporal ER rooted in a known-good present state.** Start with what you know is currently true (the FAA Part 135 list as of today), then walk backwards in time using historical datasets to discover each operator's identity chain.

This is how Senzing does it, how government agencies doing sanctions screening do it, and it's how Jonas's original NORA system did it at casinos. You anchor in the present and resolve the past.

**The workflow per operator:**

1. Take current canonical row (e.g., "Altivion Aviation, FAA cert X, registered 2025-11-02")
2. Query historical FAA snapshots → find prior names under same cert number
3. Query state registries (Delaware, Texas, Florida, Nevada, Oklahoma, etc.) → find entity filings that reference the company
4. Query DOT exemption authority records → find economic authority changes
5. Query trade press archives → find rebrand announcements, mergers, acquisitions
6. Query NTSB → find any safety events tied to any historical identity
7. Query SEC filings (for public parents) → find ownership chains
8. Query UCC filings → find aircraft liens that reveal beneficial owners
9. Query sanctions lists → check every identity variation for hits

Each query returns evidence. Your researcher agent synthesizes the evidence into the operator's temporal identity graph. You store it all with provenance. You never delete anything.

That's the method. Now the datasets.

## The datasets that actually get you to 92-97%

I'll grade each by what it gives you, what it costs, and how critical it is.

### Tier 1: Essential, free, public — get these first

**1. FAA Part 135 Operator List (monthly Excel download)**
- Free, official, updated monthly by the FAA
- Gives you: current legal name, certificate holder, certificate designator, FAA FSDO, aircraft registrations, aircraft models
- **Covers: 100% of currently-active US Part 135 operators**
- Critical: yes

**2. FAA Aircraft Registry (free, public)**
- Free CSV download at registry.faa.gov
- Gives you: every N-number, registered owner, operator of record, type certificate, airworthiness history
- Critical for aircraft-operator history — an aircraft that moved from Operator A to Operator B in 2019 is a signal those operators may have had a relationship
- **Covers: all 170K+ US-registered aircraft, with historical snapshots available**
- Critical: yes

**3. FAA Civil Aviation Registry historical snapshots**
- Available via National Archives and some research datasets
- Gives you: month-by-month or annual snapshots going back decades
- This is how you find prior names on the same cert number
- Critical: yes, but harder to acquire — you may need to archive current snapshots yourself going forward and backfill what's reconstructable

**4. DOT Economic Authority records (free)**
- transportation.gov has charter broker DOT registrations (Part 295) and air carrier certificates (Part 121, 135)
- Gives you: economic authority grants, suspensions, revocations
- Critical: yes, for tracking when an operator gained, changed, or lost economic authority

**5. State entity filings (50-state patchwork)**
- Each Secretary of State maintains a business entity database
- Gives you: LLC/Corp formation date, legal name history, registered agent, officers, mergers, dissolutions
- Free in most states, subscription in some (California charges for bulk downloads)
- **Covers: 95%+ of corporate identity chains**
- Critical: yes, this is the single biggest source for rebrand/merger evidence
- The biggest lift — you'd want Delaware, Texas, Florida, Nevada, Oklahoma, California, New York, Illinois at minimum

### Tier 2: High-value, mixed cost, fills gaps

**6. NTSB accident/incident database**
- Free, public, downloadable
- Gives you: accidents, incidents, operator attribution at time of event
- Critical for safety-record continuity across rebrands (the "classic aviation laundering rebrand" problem)
- **Covers: 100% of reportable US aviation safety events**

**7. ARGUS operator database**
- Subscription (roughly $5K-15K/year depending on tier)
- Gives you: safety ratings (Gold, Gold Plus, Platinum), audit history, fleet data
- Critical: yes for safety-tier identification, moderate for pure ER
- You're already scraping this

**8. Wyvern operator database**
- Subscription (similar tier to ARGUS)
- Gives you: Wingman certification, PASS audit data, safety metrics
- Critical: yes, same reason as ARGUS

**9. IS-BAO registry (International Standard for Business Aircraft Operations)**
- Limited public access, deeper data via subscription
- Gives you: international operator certifications, multi-jurisdiction operations
- Critical: moderate, more valuable when you expand globally

**10. UCC filings (Uniform Commercial Code)**
- State-by-state, mostly public but fragmented
- Gives you: aircraft liens, financing relationships, beneficial owner hints
- Critical: moderate, valuable for detecting ownership changes that don't show up in FAA registry

### Tier 3: Specialized, valuable for corporate intelligence

**11. SEC filings (EDGAR)**
- Free, but only covers publicly-traded parents
- Gives you: corporate ownership chains for Directional Aviation (parent of Flexjet), Surf Air Mobility, Wheels Up, Berkshire Hathaway (parent of NetJets)
- Critical: moderate, covers maybe 15% of operators by count but those 15% include the biggest players

**12. Open Ownership BODS (Beneficial Ownership Data Standard)**
- Free, open standard, coverage varies wildly by country
- Gives you: beneficial owner disclosure where governments require it (UK strong, US weak, Cayman none)
- Critical: moderate, growing in value as more jurisdictions adopt

**13. Trade press and aviation journalism archives**
- AIN, Corporate Jet Investor, Business Aviation News, Aviation International News, Private Jet Card Comparisons
- Not a single dataset — requires scraping or RSS aggregation
- Gives you: rebrand announcements, acquisition news, management changes, industry gossip
- Critical: high for rebrand detection specifically
- This is where your Hawk agent's market signals database should feed back into ER

**14. Company websites and press releases**
- Use Firecrawl to scrape "About Us" pages
- Gives you: self-reported corporate history, leadership bios, sometimes explicit "formerly known as" language
- Critical: high for direct rebrand evidence (Altivion's own site would say "formerly Aviation Advisor")

**15. LinkedIn company data and employee movement**
- Accessible via LinkedIn API with restrictions, or paid services like PhantomBuster
- Gives you: employee migration patterns that reveal real mergers (if 40 people move from Company A to Company B in one quarter, that's a merger signal)
- Critical: moderate, excellent for confirming otherwise-soft signals

### Tier 4: Deep corporate intelligence

**16. Sanctions and PEP lists (OFAC SDN, UN, EU, UK HMT, PEPs)**
- Free, public, constantly updated
- Gives you: sanctions screening across all identity variations
- Critical: yes for compliance, yes for detecting bad actors hiding behind rebrands
- Senzing has this built in

**17. CourtListener / PACER**
- Federal court filings, some free via CourtListener, PACER requires paid access
- Gives you: lawsuits that reveal corporate relationships, bankruptcies, receiverships
- Critical: moderate, occasionally reveals hidden ownership or major operator events

**18. OSINT aggregators (OpenCorporates, Sayari, etc.)**
- Paid subscriptions
- Gives you: pre-built corporate network graphs, officer overlap detection, subsidiary mapping
- Critical: moderate to high — these platforms have already done some of the graph-building work for you
- OpenCorporates has a free tier and API; Sayari is enterprise-priced

**19. FAA Form 8050-1 (aircraft registration) and Bill of Sale records**
- FAA Aircraft Registration Branch in Oklahoma City
- Gives you: aircraft transaction history, previous owners
- Critical: yes for aircraft brokerage side, moderate for operator ER

**20. International aviation registries (EASA, Transport Canada, ANAC Brazil, CAA UK, DGCA India, etc.)**
- Varying public access by jurisdiction
- Gives you: equivalent of FAA Part 135 for each country
- Critical: yes when you expand internationally, not yet for Year 1

## Now the hard truth — why you can never hit 100%

Here's what the ER literature and Senzing's 40 years of experience will tell you, and what you should internalize:

### Problem 1: Fundamentally ambiguous cases exist

Two companies with similar names, similar addresses, similar fleet composition, similar pilots — but they're genuinely two different companies. OR: Two companies with completely different names, different addresses, different fleets — but they're legally the same entity through a holding company restructure.

**No amount of data solves this if the ground truth itself is ambiguous.** Legal identity can be genuinely unclear. Is a holding company with two AOC subsidiaries "one operator" or "two operators"? Depends on your question. The answer is context-dependent, not data-dependent.

### Problem 2: Private companies can legally obscure themselves

Delaware allows anonymous LLC formation. Cayman registration doesn't require beneficial owner disclosure. A company can genuinely be structured so that connecting it to its ultimate owner is not possible with public data.

**This is by design.** Privacy-preserving corporate structures exist for legitimate reasons (and illegitimate ones). You cannot resolve what regulators have agreed should not be resolvable.

### Problem 3: Historical data has gaps

Pre-2000 FAA records are incomplete. State SOS records pre-1990s are often paper-only or destroyed. Trade press from before internet archiving is lost. NTSB attribution errors from the 1970s-80s exist in the database and can't be retroactively fixed.

**The further back you go, the thinner the evidence, the more you're making probabilistic guesses dressed as resolutions.**

### Problem 4: Genuine adversarial actors

Some operators specifically engineer their identity chains to evade resolution. Fraudulent operators, post-crash reorganizers, operators under DOT enforcement actions who dissolve and reform. **They are actively trying to defeat your ER.** You can raise the cost of evasion, you cannot eliminate it.

### Problem 5: Resolution is not a binary

"Is Company A the same as Company B?" is often not yes/no. It's "they share 80% operational continuity but different legal entity and 60% personnel change." Different questions about them will correctly get different answers. Your ER system has to embrace this ambiguity, not pretend it doesn't exist.

## What "good" actually looks like

Based on published benchmarks from the ER literature:

- **Senzing's claimed accuracy: 99%+ on structured fields** (names, addresses, SSNs, DOB) when data is clean
- **Multi-agent LLM ER (MDPI 2025): 94.3%** on name variations in test data
- **Human expert review: usually 96-98%** on hard cases

**For your aviation-specific ER, realistic target benchmarks:**

- **Auto-merge tier (high confidence):** 97-99% precision. These are the "ABC Aviation LLC" = "ABC Aviation, Inc." matches where certificate number, address, and fleet all agree.
- **Review tier (mid confidence):** 90-95% precision post-human-review. The "Altivion = Aviation Advisor" category.
- **Overall system precision at your 2-year target:** **95-97%.** Good enough that Dumont can quote operators with confidence. Not 100%.

The remaining 3-5% gets manually curated as edge cases surface. Over time, your ontology accumulates specific "we already decided X and Y are the same" decisions with evidence, so that specific pair never needs to be re-resolved.

## What you should actually do, concretely

Step-by-step from where you are:

### Phase 1 (ongoing): Data ingestion pipeline
- [ ] Ingest full FAA Part 135 list monthly (automated)
- [ ] Ingest FAA Aircraft Registry monthly (automated, you have this)
- [ ] Ingest NTSB accident/incident data (automated, free)
- [ ] Build state SOS scraper for Delaware, Texas, Florida, Nevada, Oklahoma, California, NY, Illinois (this is 1-2 weeks of engineering work, high leverage)
- [ ] Archive current snapshots forever so future-you has historical data (start today if you haven't)

### Phase 2: Commercial data integration
- [ ] Maintain ARGUS and Wyvern scrapes (you have this)
- [ ] Add OpenCorporates API (free tier exists) for initial beneficial owner data
- [ ] Add OFAC SDN sanctions screening (free, federal)

### Phase 3: Research agent layer
- [ ] Build the Firecrawl-powered researcher agent for ambiguous cases
- [ ] Connect Hawk's market signals DB to feed rebrand/merger signals back to ER review queue
- [ ] Multi-model verification on Gold merges (Opus + Sonnet + GPT)

### Phase 4: Historical backfill
- [ ] For each of the 1,821 current operators, walk backwards using the datasets above
- [ ] Expected output: ~4,000-7,000 identity rows total (each operator has 2-4 historical identities on average)
- [ ] Expected data quality: 95-97% precision after researcher review

### Phase 5: Continuous improvement
- [ ] Every Dumont deal generates new observations that update the ER graph
- [ ] Every review queue decision trains the researcher
- [ ] Over 6-12 months, auto-merge tier precision climbs from 87% to 95%+

## The question behind the question

When you ask "can we get 100% ER" I think you're really asking: *is the ER effort worth it if it's never complete?*

Yes. **Completeness is not the goal. Reliability-within-scope is the goal.**

A 95% accurate ER for the 1,821 US operators that Dumont queries every day is infinitely more valuable than a hypothetical 100% ER that doesn't exist. JETNET built a $100M+ business on less complete data than you'll have by the end of Phase 1 of this plan.

The competitive advantage isn't perfect resolution. It's that you're the only aviation company with a researcher-agent-backed, continuously-updating, provenance-tracked, multi-source-verified ER graph — while everyone else is still calling operators on the phone or paying JETNET six figures a year for stale data.

## Claude

Good question. Let me give you the honest answer — this matters because it tells you what OSA's eventual moat around bank/insurer data sales actually costs to build.

## What JETNET actually sells to banks and insurers

First, let's be clear what they're selling, because the compliance requirements flow from the product category. From JETNET's own site, their Aviation Finance customer categories are:

- **Banks** — Streamline dissemination of aircraft, fleet and owner documents and data
- **Insurers** — Discover fragmented, disparate, and hidden aviation documents and data in a click
- **Lenders** — Assess the risk profile and performance of underlying assets
- **Aircraft Title Services** — Unearth and validate ownership, chain of custody, and encumbrances
- **NBFI** (Non-Bank Financial Institutions)

What they're selling is **market intelligence data, ownership/title records, transaction history, and valuation data** — not customer PII, not financial account data, not regulated consumer information.

**This matters enormously for the compliance picture.** JETNET is a B2B data vendor to financial institutions. They are not a financial institution themselves. They don't underwrite loans, issue policies, or hold consumer accounts. Their compliance burden is therefore much lighter than, say, Plaid or a credit bureau.

## The actual compliance stack JETNET almost certainly has

JETNET doesn't publish their compliance posture publicly (I couldn't find a published SOC 2 report, ISO certification, or trust page). But based on what's required to contract with banks and insurers as a data vendor, here's what they realistically hold:

### The ones that are table stakes for enterprise B2B data sales

**1. SOC 2 Type II** — almost certainly yes

This is the single most important one. Large enterprise customers often require their financial services providers and data centers to maintain SOC 2 compliance before signing contracts. The attestation demonstrates that an organization has the controls and processes in place to protect sensitive financial data throughout its lifecycle.

SOC 2 is an AICPA-defined attestation framework. There is no official SOC 2 certification. However, organizations can receive a SOC 2 attestation report verified by an independent auditor, such as a Certified Public Accountant (CPA) licensed by AICPA, to achieve SOC 2 compliance successfully.

- **Type I** is a point-in-time snapshot — "at this moment, your controls are designed correctly"
- **Type II** covers a period (usually 6-12 months) — "your controls actually operated effectively over time"

Banks and insurers typically require Type II, not Type I, because Type I is easy to game. Type II proves ongoing operational discipline.

No serious bank vendor risk management team signs a data contract without reviewing a SOC 2 Type II report. JETNET has customers like Bombardier, Cessna, and likely the major aviation-specific lenders (Global Jet Capital, PNC Aviation Finance, 1st Source Bank's aircraft finance group, Wells Fargo's specialty lending arm). Those customers absolutely require SOC 2 Type II from their data vendors.

**2. Vendor risk management documentation**

Beyond SOC 2, each enterprise customer runs its own due diligence:
- Security questionnaires (SIG, CAIQ)
- Business continuity plans
- Disaster recovery plans
- Incident response procedures
- Data classification policies
- Access control documentation
- Encryption standards (in transit, at rest)
- Penetration test reports (usually annual)

This isn't a certification per se — it's hundreds of hours per year answering bank procurement teams. JETNET almost certainly has a dedicated vendor management contact.

### The ones that become relevant at scale

**3. ISO 27001** — possibly yes, especially for European customers

ISO 27001 is the international equivalent of SOC 2 and is more respected in European banking contexts (Commerzbank, Deutsche Bank, Barclays, BNP Paribas — all common aircraft finance lenders). SOC compliance helps companies comply with other regulatory bodies, including HIPAA, GDPR, ISO 27001, etc. Moreover, it shares similar requirements to ISO 27001 guidelines.

If JETNET sells meaningfully in Europe (they do — their customer base is global), they likely hold ISO 27001 or are working toward it.

**4. GDPR compliance** — yes, legally required if they touch any EU data

Any aircraft owner, broker, or contact who is an EU resident is a "data subject" under GDPR. JETNET's database includes global aircraft ownership data. They have legal exposure and must have GDPR-compliant data processing agreements, privacy notices, and data subject rights mechanisms.

### The ones that do NOT apply to JETNET (important)

This is where most people get confused. JETNET does **not** have to comply with:

**GLBA (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act)** — GLBA applies to financial institutions that collect non-public personal information from consumers. JETNET doesn't serve consumers. They serve businesses. GLBA does not apply to them as a vendor to financial institutions, though they may contractually inherit GLBA-type obligations through bank vendor agreements.

**FCRA (Fair Credit Reporting Act)** — JETNET is not a consumer reporting agency. They provide aircraft data, not consumer credit data. FCRA doesn't apply.

**PCI-DSS** — They don't process credit cards for consumers. Not applicable.

**HIPAA** — Not a healthcare entity. Not applicable.

**SEC regulations** — They're not a broker-dealer, investment advisor, or market data provider for securities. Not applicable.

**FDIC / OCC banking regulations** — They're not a bank. Not applicable directly, but their bank customers flow certain requirements down through vendor contracts.

## What this means for OSA's eventual bank/insurance data strategy

Now the real question — what do **you** need to build toward?

### Phase 0 (current, through Year 2 of OSA)
**Zero compliance infrastructure needed.** You're selling to clients and working with operators — not selling data to regulated financial institutions. Focus on the business.

### Phase 1 (Year 2-3, when you start thinking about data products)
Start tracking compliance hygiene passively:
- Document everything: data sources, access controls, decision logs
- Use infrastructure that's already SOC 2 compliant (Supabase ✓, AWS ✓, Vercel ✓, Anthropic ✓)
- Maintain clean audit trails — you're already doing this with your "never delete claims" rule
- Keep vendor contracts clean
- Don't process PII you don't need

### Phase 2 (Year 3-4, when data becomes a revenue line)
**Begin SOC 2 Type II journey.** Realistic timeline and cost:
- **Prep: 6-9 months** (policies, procedures, control implementation)
- **Type I audit: 1-2 months** after prep is done
- **Type II observation window: 6-12 months** after Type I
- **Total time: ~12-18 months** from "we want to pursue this" to "we have a Type II report in hand"
- **Cost: $40,000-$120,000** for the audit + external prep help, depending on scope and auditor. Can be cheaper with platforms like Vanta, Drata, or Secureframe ($15K-30K for the platform plus audit fees).

### Phase 3 (Year 4-5+, when you're selling to banks and insurers)
Add on as needed:
- ISO 27001 if expanding internationally (~$50K-100K incremental if already SOC 2)
- Specific bank vendor certifications (each bank has its own)
- Data processing agreements tailored to each customer
- Penetration testing (annual, ~$25K-75K)
- Cyber insurance (mandatory for any bank vendor contract, ~$25K-100K/year)

**Total compliance cost at Phase 3 maturity: $150K-400K per year.** That's the price of selling data to banks and insurers. JETNET pays this. Palantir pays this. Any enterprise data vendor to financial institutions pays this.

## The strategic framing that matters

Here's where I'd push back on the framing of your question a bit, because I think the strategic picture is more interesting than the pure compliance picture:

**The compliance cost is not the barrier to entry for OSA. The data is.**

JETNET's moat isn't their SOC 2 Type II report. Every serious competitor can get SOC 2. JETNET's moat is 35+ years of continuously collected, verified, de-duplicated aviation transaction data with confirmed sale prices, ownership chains, and relationship intelligence. That's what banks and insurers pay for.

Your moat potential is **better data**:
- Real-time operator intelligence (JETNET is minutes-behind-FAA, you could be seconds-behind-ADS-B)
- Charter pricing intelligence (JETNET has zero presence here — they know aircraft values, not charter rates)
- Relationship graph (you're building what they've been building by hand for decades, but with AI from Day 1)
- Safety-continuity tracking across rebrands (they don't do this well — your entity resolution graph specifically addresses this)

**When you're ready to sell to banks and insurers, the compliance is the last 6 months of work, not the first.** You build the data first. Then you make it enterprise-sellable.

Here's how this actually plays out for OSA:

1. **Year 1-2:** Close charter deals. Ignore bank/insurance data sales entirely.
2. **Year 2-3:** Aircraft brokerage starts generating transaction data. Your ER graph matures. You start noticing that your data is richer than what exists elsewhere.
3. **Year 3:** Someone from a bank or insurer asks "can I pay for access to your data?" — this is the signal. Don't initiate this.

This matches JETNET's actual history. They didn't start as a bank data vendor. They started as aircraft transaction data for dealers and brokers. Banks came to them because the data was uniquely good. Compliance followed demand.
